sales-flow.title: BA Sales
sales-flow.subtitle: Keep your pipeline moving.
sales-flow.intro: Connect your CRM and inbox to organize incoming leads, maintain sales records and coordinate follow-up. The service prepares quotes, proposals and suggested next steps using your agreed sales process. You receive a clearer pipeline, regular reporting and drafts ready for review, while routine activity follows the rules agreed at setup.
inclusions: Lead qualification and scoring against agreed criteria.
Sales forecasts and reports based on available pipeline data.
sales-flow.control: Quotes, proposals and new offers come to you for approval. Routine follow-ups run within agreed rules; requests outside those rules are escalated for your decision.
sales-flow.whoItSuits: Businesses that want consistent follow-up and a clearer view of their sales pipeline.
sales-flow.example: A lead arrives overnight. Its details are organized in your CRM, scored against your criteria and paired with a suggested next step for review.
sales-flow.scope: Supported CRM and inbox connections, messaging rules and workflow coverage are confirmed before setup.

customer-support.title: BA Customer Service
customer-support.subtitle: Give every enquiry a clear next step.
customer-support.intro: Connect supported helpdesk, inbox and agreed customer-service channels to organize enquiries and coordinate responses. The service uses your approved knowledge and policies to answer routine questions, track tickets and identify cases needing a person. You receive a more consistent support workflow, with exceptions and sensitive decisions brought to your attention.
inclusions: Routine enquiry handling across agreed phone, email and chat connections.
Order and service issue handling within approved policies.
Return and refund preparation for approval.
customer-support.control: Refunds, returns and exceptions outside approved policies are referred for your decision. Unverified answers are escalated rather than presented as facts.
customer-support.whoItSuits: Businesses that need consistent support as enquiry volumes grow.
customer-support.example: A customer asks about a delayed order. The service checks the connected order record and provides the available status, or routes the case for investigation when information is missing.
customer-support.scope: Channels, knowledge sources, coverage hours and escalation arrangements are agreed before launch.

operational-intelligence.title: BA Finance
operational-intelligence.subtitle: Keep everyday finance organized.
operational-intelligence.intro: Connect supported accounting software and financial data sources to coordinate invoicing, payment tracking and routine finance administration. The service prepares records, highlights exceptions and brings payroll, payables and reporting together for review. You receive a clearer financial picture while decisions involving payments or sensitive changes remain within your approval rules.
inclusions: Invoice preparation and sending under agreed rules.
Payment collection workflows through approved payment tools.
Incoming and outgoing payment records and reconciliation support.
Invoice-tax application using your confirmed configuration.
operational-intelligence.control: Payroll, payables and sensitive financial actions require approval. Tax settings and accounting judgments require appropriate review; automation does not replace your accountant's professional judgment.
operational-intelligence.whoItSuits: Owners who want coordinated invoicing, collections, expenses and reporting with less repetitive administration.
operational-intelligence.example: Upcoming bills and recorded income indicate a possible cash shortfall. The service flags it so you can review timing and take action.
operational-intelligence.scope: Available feeds, reconciliation frequency and payment permissions are confirmed during setup.

managed-it.title: BA IT
managed-it.subtitle: Keep routine technology work under control.
managed-it.intro: Connect supported systems to coordinate maintenance, helpdesk work and everyday IT administration. The service tracks issues, prepares or performs permitted routine actions and flags changes that need review. You receive maintenance visibility and exception reporting, with critical-system changes handled through agreed controls.
inclusions: Backup operation and verification within the agreed scope.
managed-it.control: Critical-system changes and sensitive access actions require approval. Routine changes follow agreed maintenance windows, verification and recovery procedures.
managed-it.whoItSuits: Businesses needing structured routine IT support and clearer ownership of recurring technical tasks.
managed-it.example: A relevant patch becomes available. The service identifies affected systems and prepares the update for the agreed testing and approval process.
managed-it.scope: Supported systems, backup verification depth and maintenance coverage are agreed before launch. This does not automatically include specialist cybersecurity or forensic response.

customer-growth.title: BA Marketing
customer-growth.subtitle: Turn your marketing plan into consistent activity.
customer-growth.intro: Coordinate content, email, social and advertising workflows through your supported accounts. The service prepares material in your brand voice, organizes your calendar and reports on campaign activity. You review publication and spending decisions, while approved work proceeds within the agreed plan.
inclusions: Social scheduling and publication after approval.
Email campaigns and newsletters for eligible audiences.
customer-growth.control: Public material requires approval before publication. Spending follows your approved budget; proposed increases require a new decision. Audience permissions and unsubscribe preferences must be respected.
customer-growth.whoItSuits: Businesses seeking a consistent marketing cadence without managing every repetitive step themselves.
customer-growth.example: Research identifies a relevant market change. The service drafts a campaign adjustment and supporting content for your review before anything is published.
customer-growth.scope: Channels, content volumes, ad accounts and publishing permissions are agreed at setup. Search rankings and campaign results are not guaranteed.

tailored.title: BA Tailored Automation
tailored.subtitle: Automate a workflow unique to your business.
tailored.intro: Describe a repetitive task that does not fit the standard BA services. We assess the workflow, confirm the inputs and decisions it needs, and scope an automation around that specific process. You receive a tested workflow with defined boundaries, exception handling and approval points.
inclusions: Review of the task and its suitability for automation.
Identification of required data, software connections and owners.
A defined scope covering included actions and exclusions.
Build and testing against the agreed workflow.
A quotation based on the confirmed scope.
tailored.control: Sensitive actions and exceptions follow agreed approval rules. Changes beyond the agreed workflow are reviewed before implementation.
tailored.whoItSuits: Businesses with a specific recurring task that does not fit a standard package.
tailored.example: A property manager needs maintenance requests matched to suitable contractors. A tailored workflow prepares matches using job type and available information, with exceptions referred for review.
tailored.scope: Custom quotation. A request spanning a broader connected operation may be better suited to OR ONE; this is assessed before committing to a build.

professionalServices.name: Professional Services
professionalServices.overview: Accounting and bookkeeping firms sit at the centre of their clients’ financial lives—tax filings, payroll records, banking details and, often, authority to move client money. That concentration of sensitive data and payment authority makes firms a high-value target, independent of size.
risks: Business email compromise and fraudulent banking-detail changes
Account takeover across email and cloud-accounting platforms
Unmanaged remote devices and unreviewed third-party access
Backup and recovery gaps affecting client financial records
Weak SPF, DKIM or DMARC enforcement
priorities: MFA on every email and cloud-accounting account
DMARC moved from monitoring to full enforcement
Regular staff and vendor access reviews
Tested backups and documented security awareness

jobs.why: Keep every referral, enquiry, proposal and engagement-letter follow-up moving—even through busy season.
Turn scattered firm data into a current view of capacity, realization and client profitability.

professionalServices.unify: When new-client intake, engagement and billing, staff capacity and client communication must move as one coordinated system—not as separate automations—that is OR ONE territory.

detail.context: PIPEDA may require safeguards appropriate to the sensitivity of personal information, breach reporting where there is a real risk of significant harm, notification, and breach records. Provincial privacy and professional rules may also apply. Accounting, legal and advisory firms should confirm their exact obligations during scoping.
protect: Enforce MFA across email, cloud, accounting and privileged accounts.
Validate legitimate senders before moving SPF, DKIM and DMARC toward enforcement.
Independently verify payment instructions and banking-detail changes.
Review staff, contractor and vendor access at departures and on a defined schedule.
Protect client-document exchange, test backup restoration and document incident response.
automate: Sales for referrals, proposals and engagement follow-up.
Secure client intake with document-status tracking and approved onboarding steps.
Finance for capacity, work in progress, billing and client-service visibility.
detail.question: What is the most common practical cyber risk for a professional-services firm?
detail.answer: Compromised email and identity are high-leverage risks because they can expose confidential information and enable convincing payment or account-change fraud.

healthcare.name: Healthcare
healthcare.overview: Clinics work across scheduling, EMR, billing and communication systems maintained by several vendors, while staff turnover creates recurring access-control work around highly sensitive patient information.
risks: Phishing aimed at front-desk and billing teams
Weak separation between clinical and administrative access
priorities: MFA across clinical and billing systems
Access reviews during every staff change
Managed protection for every connected endpoint

jobs.why: Improve high-volume scheduling, intake and follow-up communication.
Keep scheduling and records systems dependable without building a full internal IT team.

healthcare.unify: When patient intake, billing, staff scheduling and communication must coordinate across providers or locations, the need has moved into OR ONE territory.

detail.context: In Ontario, PHIPA governs health information custodians and their agents. Custodians remain responsible when third-party providers are used, and breach notification and annual statistical reporting duties can apply. Other provinces have their own health-privacy regimes.
protect: Enforce MFA for clinical, billing, remote and privileged accounts.
Use role-based access and review it after every staffing change.
Manage and patch every endpoint that touches patient information.
Test restoration of critical systems and maintain downtime procedures.
Review vendor safeguards, access, breach notice and data-disposition terms.
automate: Approved reminders, intake status and non-clinical follow-up with staff escalation.
Administrative intake that checks completeness without automating clinical decisions.
IT for endpoint health, tickets, device lifecycle and recurring access work.
detail.question: Does a cloud healthcare vendor take privacy responsibility away from an Ontario clinic?
detail.answer: No. Ontario guidance makes clear that a custodian remains responsible for personal health information in its custody or control, including when providers are involved.

financialServices.name: Financial Services
financialServices.overview: Financial firms handle regulated data, high-value transactions and third-party platforms while maintaining evidence and audit trails as part of everyday operations.
risks: Custodian, lender and CRM vendor risk

jobs.why: Create dependable visibility across reporting, portfolio and pipeline data.
Maintain monitored, dependable infrastructure around critical workflows.

financialServices.unify: When compliance reporting, client communication and advisor operations need one coordinated, auditable system, that becomes OR ONE territory.

detail.context: The applicable framework depends on the activity. OSFI B-13 and B-10 apply to federally regulated financial institutions, not every financial SMB. FINTRAC applies to defined reporting entities and covered activities. Provincial, contractual and professional rules may also apply.
protect: Use strong MFA for privileged, email, financial and remote accounts.
Separate and monitor administrative privilege.
Require independent verification for payment and account-detail changes.
Maintain vendor inventories, risk assessments, contract controls and exit plans.
Test incident response, continuity and recovery around critical workflows.
automate: Compliance workflow support for evidence, review, exceptions and approvals.
Controlled client onboarding with required human review.
Finance for authorized pipeline, service, exception and risk views.
detail.question: Does OSFI Guideline B-13 apply to every Canadian financial business?
detail.answer: No. B-13 applies to federally regulated financial institutions. Other financial businesses may face different federal, provincial, contractual or professional obligations.

retail.name: Retail & E-commerce
retail.overview: Retail and e-commerce operators manage payment data, seasonal demand and an always-on customer journey across marketing, checkout, fulfilment and support.

jobs.why: Strengthen repeat purchases, retention and reactivation at scale.
Keep leads and abandonment follow-up moving without manual effort.

retail.unify: When marketing, sales, fulfilment and customer support must operate as one connected system across channels, that is OR ONE territory.

detail.context: Canadian privacy law may govern customer information. PCI DSS is a payment-card industry standard, not Canadian legislation. PCI DSS v4.0.1 includes e-commerce attention to payment-page scripts and change or tamper detection.
protect: Enforce MFA for store administration, email, payments and remote access.
Minimize storage and exposure of payment and personal information.
Control plug-ins, scripts, integrations and updates.
Monitor payment-page changes, public applications, APIs and availability.
Review third-party access and test restoration before peak periods.
automate: Customer Service for approved answers, routing and human escalation.
Marketing for consent-aware post-purchase, loyalty and reactivation journeys.
Finance for inventory, fulfilment, returns and campaign visibility.
detail.question: Is PCI DSS a Canadian privacy law?
detail.answer: No. PCI DSS is a payment-card industry security standard. Canadian privacy laws may separately govern the personal information a retailer handles.

manufacturing.name: Manufacturing
manufacturing.overview: Manufacturers combine office IT, production-adjacent systems, legacy equipment and supplier access—where an ordinary technology incident can become measurable production downtime.
risks: Weak separation between office and production systems

jobs.why: Tie infrastructure reliability directly to production continuity.
Replace delayed inventory, supplier and production reporting with a current view.

manufacturing.unify: When supply-chain, inventory and operating data need one coordinated planning-and-execution system, the requirement becomes OR ONE.

detail.context: Canadian cyber guidance highlights supply-chain threats, ransomware and risk-based security for smaller organizations. Exact duties depend on products, customers, safety, export controls, critical-infrastructure role and the information handled.
protect: Inventory IT, OT, connected equipment, remote paths and critical dependencies.
Separate business and production environments where feasible.
Use approved, time-limited and monitored vendor access.
Prioritize vulnerabilities by exposure, exploitability, safety and production impact.
Test recovery for business systems and production-critical configurations.
automate: IT for endpoints, access, service requests and recurring evidence.
Finance for authorized inventory, quality, downtime and supplier indicators.
Supplier workflows for approvals, evidence, expiry dates and exceptions.
detail.question: Why is vendor access a major manufacturing cyber risk?
detail.answer: Permanent, excessive or unmonitored supplier access can create a path into business or production environments when a vendor identity or system is compromised.

technology.name: Technology
technology.overview: Technology companies often scale revenue and headcount faster than internal process, accumulating SaaS tools, integrations and inconsistent access governance along the way.

jobs.why: Scale pipeline execution without scaling administration at the same rate.
Connect product, customer and revenue information into current decisions.

technology.unify: When sales, product data and customer operations require one system rather than a growing collection of tools, that is OR ONE territory.

detail.context: Privacy, customer contracts, insurer conditions and supply-chain requirements all matter. Canada's proposed Artificial Intelligence and Data Act should not be described as enacted law; current advice should focus on privacy, security, approved use, human oversight and accountability.
protect: Centralize identity, enforce MFA and control joiner, mover and leaver events.
Protect cloud administration, source code, CI/CD and secrets.
Establish secure development, dependency, vulnerability and release practices.
Inventory APIs, integrations, data flows and third-party components.
Define approved AI uses, prohibited data and human-review requirements.
automate: Sales for demand, qualification, proposals and handoff.
Customer Service for approved knowledge, routing and escalation.
Finance for product, service, customer and revenue indicators.
detail.question: Is Canada's proposed Artificial Intelligence and Data Act currently law?
detail.answer: No. Technology companies should still establish practical AI governance around privacy, security, approved use, human oversight and accountability.

construction.name: Construction & Real Estate
construction.overview: Construction and real-estate businesses coordinate office, field and site teams through email, mobile devices and a mix of project, transaction and client-management systems.
risks: Inconsistent access across sites and teams

jobs.why: Support a distributed workforce and its devices reliably.
Maintain disciplined follow-up across long buyer, tenant and client cycles.

construction.unify: When project management, client communication and back-office finance need to coordinate across multiple sites or listings, that is OR ONE territory.

detail.context: Real-estate brokers, representatives and developers can have FINTRAC duties when performing covered activities. Obligations differ by entity and activity. Privacy and contract requirements may also apply.
protect: Enforce MFA across email, project, property, finance and remote systems.
Independently verify payment and banking-detail changes.
Manage mobile devices and protect business information.
Give contractors time-bound, least-privilege access.
Review access at project completion and retain required records.
automate: Sales for enquiries, appointments, proposals and long-cycle follow-up.
Project intake for approved documents, missing items, routing and status.
IT for distributed devices, accounts and recurring service work.
detail.question: Do all Canadian construction and real-estate businesses have the same FINTRAC obligations?
detail.answer: No. Obligations depend on the entity and activities performed; covered businesses must assess the current guidance specific to them.

education.name: Education
education.overview: Education providers hold student and family data across administrative and learning systems while handling a constant volume of communication with parents, students and staff.
risks: Inconsistent access across learning and admin systems

jobs.why: Handle repeat parent and student enquiries more consistently.
Support administrative and learning systems as one dependable environment.

education.unify: When admissions, communication and administration must coordinate across programs or campuses, the operating need becomes OR ONE.

detail.context: Privacy duties depend on province and whether the institution is public or private. Ontario regulator findings on PowerSchool emphasize vendor oversight, contractual safeguards and continued responsibility for information in an institution's custody or control.
protect: Enforce MFA for staff, administrators, remote and privileged accounts.
Review roles as students, staff and contractors enter or leave.
Protect endpoints, especially administrator and shared devices.
Assess education-technology vendors, contracts, access and data disposition.
Test restoration and maintain learning-continuity and incident plans.
automate: Approved routine information and support with escalation to staff.
Admissions administration for document status, reminders and authorized handoffs.
IT for devices, accounts, tickets and access work.
detail.question: Does an education organization transfer privacy responsibility to its software provider?
detail.answer: Not automatically. Applicable law and organization type matter, but recent Ontario findings emphasize active vendor oversight and continued responsibility.

otherSmbs.name: Other Canadian SMBs
otherSmbs.overview: Businesses that do not fit a named vertical still rely on the same essentials: email, cloud tools, a handful of vendors and operating work that is often more manual than it needs to be.

jobs.why: Create a dependable path from enquiry to close.
Respond, route and follow up consistently as demand grows.

otherSmbs.unify: When sales, support and operations genuinely need to run as one coordinated system rather than separate functions, that is OR ONE territory.

detail.context: PIPEDA can apply to personal information handled in commercial activity. Alberta, British Columbia and Quebec have substantially similar private-sector laws, while sector and provincial duties may also apply. Canadian baseline controls offer a practical risk-based starting point.
protect: Document critical assets, accounts, data and vendors.
Enforce MFA across email, cloud, finance and administration.
Manage endpoints, updates, backups and privileged access.
Protect email and train staff around phishing and payment fraud.
Test recovery and define incident decision ownership.
automate: Sales workflows so enquiries and proposals do not go cold.
Customer Service for consistent routing, answers and escalation.
Finance for governed, current reporting.
IT for routine devices, accounts, tickets and access.
detail.question: Where should a Canadian SMB begin with cybersecurity?
detail.answer: Begin with a risk baseline covering critical accounts, devices, data, vendors, backups and business processes, then prioritize MFA, email protection, managed updates and tested recovery.

items.q: How do I choose which services I need?
items.a: Pick what you already know you need, or use Not sure — help me choose. Our team will help you find the right starting point without guessing.

items.q: Do I need to talk to someone before I sign up?
items.a: No. You can use email, ORAGROL chat, the website form or meet in person. A conversation is only needed when you want one or the service requires custom scoping.

items.q: What if I want to talk to someone before deciding?
items.a: ORAGROL chat is available 24/7. A real person is available Monday to Friday, 9am to 6pm ET, subject to availability.

items.q: What happens after I reach out?
items.a: We confirm what you need and prepare a proposal covering the appropriate scope.

items.q: How do you prepare a proposal?
items.a: We use the products or services you selected to define scope, pricing and terms for your review.

items.q: What is in the contract?
items.a: The exact products or services ordered, conditions, amount, payment method and both sides’ responsibilities.

items.q: How do I sign and confirm?
items.a: You review, sign and return the contract. We finalize it before the order is confirmed.

items.q: When and how do I pay?
items.a: Payment follows the signed contract, never before. It is due according to the terms stated there.

items.q: Do I get an invoice?
items.a: Yes. Once the signed contract and payment are received, we issue a complete invoice for the order.

items.q: What payment methods do you accept?
items.a: Card or bank transfer, as stated in your contract.

items.q: Is GST or HST shown separately?
items.a: Yes. Applicable tax is shown as a separate line on your invoice.

items.q: What happens if a payment is late?
items.a: Invoices are due within 30 days. Unpaid balances accrue interest at 1.5% per month, and service may be paused when payment is more than 15 days overdue.

items.q: Can I cancel or change services later?
items.a: Yes. With 60 days’ written notice and no outstanding balance, there is no cancellation fee. Other cancellation costs and OR ONE term conditions are defined in the contract.

items.q: What happens to my data if I cancel?
items.a: Under our standard agreement, data is returned or securely destroyed within 30 days, with written certification available on request.

items.q: What guarantees do you offer?
items.a: Action-taking services state target response times. They remain targets, not guarantees, until proven in live operation.

items.q: What are my responsibilities and yours?
items.a: Both sides’ responsibilities are written explicitly into the contract before signing.

items.q: Is this just a security report?
items.a: No. Most services are designed to take action, while selected services provide ongoing expert oversight and advice.

items.q: Who does the work?
items.a: Detection and analysis can run automatically around the clock. Nothing reaches you and no action is taken without human review.

items.q: How fast do you respond to a real problem?
items.a: Each action-taking service has a stated target response time. The applicable target appears with the service.

items.q: What access do you need?
items.a: Primarily read access and, for action-taking services, limited write access to approved business systems. Access can start narrow and expand when appropriate.

items.q: Is this one-time or ongoing?
items.a: Most services provide ongoing protection rather than a one-time checkup.

items.q: What do I receive?
items.a: Clear visibility into findings, fixes and open items, plus urgent alerts. Delivery begins through written summaries and email, with a fuller online dashboard planned.

items.q: Do I need a technical background?
items.a: No. Information is written for business owners and decision-makers.

items.q: Will dangerous findings be flagged immediately?
items.a: Yes. Urgent findings are not held for a scheduled update.

items.q: What if something is not working?
items.a: Reach us through ORAGROL chat or email and our team will review it.

items.q: How fast do you respond to support?
items.a: Urgent issues for active clients follow the target stated in their service. General questions are handled the same or next business day.

items.q: Do you offer support outside business hours?
items.a: ORAGROL chat is available 24/7. Human support is Monday to Friday, 9am to 6pm ET, subject to availability.

items.q: Can chat help with an active incident if I am not a client?
items.a: Chat can route your message, but it is not emergency incident response and does not create a service relationship. It does not provide remediation instructions.

items.q: How do I reach ORAGROL?
items.a: Use ORAGROL chat or the contact form. Department mailboxes will be published once the permanent domain is active.

items.q: Where are you located?
items.a: Headquarters and Registered Office: Thunder Bay, Ontario. Toronto Presence: Toronto, Ontario.

items.q: Can I talk to a real person?
items.a: Yes, Monday to Friday, 9am to 6pm ET, subject to availability.

items.q: Is my data safe?
items.a: We handle data in line with Canadian privacy law and require appropriate insurance before taking on client-system access.

items.q: How much does it cost?
items.a: Starting prices appear on each service page. Your exact cost depends on the selected Cybersecurity, Business Automation or OR ONE scope.

items.q: What if we outgrow our plan?
items.a: Cybersecurity tiers and Business Automation packages can be upgraded, while OR ONE scales into custom requirements.

items.q: Do you replace our IT provider?
items.a: Usually no. We work alongside existing IT providers or internal teams, focusing on the security and automation layer.

items.q: Which industries do you serve?
items.a: We support Canadian small and medium-sized businesses across the industry profiles shown on our Industries page.

questions.text: Does everyone in the business use a different password for each work account, instead of reusing the same one everywhere?
Are default passwords changed immediately when new devices or software are set up?
Do employees sign in using a password plus a code from their phone or an authenticator app for email and other important accounts?
Is MFA required for anyone who can access company systems or data from outside the office?
Does your email system filter out spam and suspicious messages before they reach employee inboxes?
Have employees received any training on spotting phishing emails in the past 12 months?
Is there a simple way for employees to report a suspicious email so it can be checked?
Do all company computers have antivirus or anti-malware software installed and actively running?
Are company laptops and desktops set to automatically lock after a short period of inactivity?
Are software and operating system updates installed automatically, or within a few days of release?
Has your business confirmed that all software and hardware currently in use is still supported with security updates?
Is your business data backed up automatically on a regular schedule (daily or more frequently)?
Has a backup restore actually been tested in the past 12 months, not just the backup itself?
If ransomware locked every file tomorrow, are you confident the business could recover without paying?
Is your office Wi-Fi password-protected and kept separate from any guest network?
Does your business use a firewall to help protect its network from outside threats?
Are security features like 2-Step Verification and suspicious sign-in alerts turned on in your Google Workspace admin settings?
Does someone check periodically who has access to shared Google Drive files and folders?
Are security features like multi-factor sign-in and suspicious login alerts turned on in whatever cloud email/file system you use?
Does someone check periodically who has access to shared files and folders in your cloud system?
Have employees received any form of cybersecurity awareness training?
Is there a simple written policy employees can refer to for using company technology safely?
Do employees generally only have access to the files and systems they actually need for their job?
Is an employee's system access removed promptly when they leave the company?
Are company-owned phones and tablets protected with a passcode or fingerprint/face lock?
If a company mobile device were lost or stolen, could it be remotely locked or wiped?
Do employees working remotely connect to company systems through a secure or VPN connection?
Are personal devices used to access company data required to meet basic security standards, like a passcode and updated software?
Is sensitive business or customer data stored only in approved systems, rather than personal email or personal cloud drives?
Is sensitive data encrypted when it's stored or sent to others?
Do you know which outside vendors or contractors currently have access to your systems or data?
Are you aware of any security practices your key vendors follow to protect shared data?
Does your website use HTTPS (the padlock icon shown in the browser address bar)?
Is your website, and any customer login area, kept updated and monitored?
If you accept card payments, do you use a PCI-compliant payment processor rather than storing card details yourself?
Is access to online banking and financial systems limited to a small number of trusted people?
Does your business have any plan for what to do if you suspect a cyberattack or data breach?
Would employees know exactly who to contact immediately if something looked suspicious?
Is access to servers, network equipment, or sensitive paperwork restricted to authorized staff only?
Are computer screens locked or logged off when employees step away from their desks?
Has a specific person or role been assigned responsibility for cybersecurity decisions in the business?
Is cybersecurity spending or investment reviewed at least once a year?
Does your business currently carry a cyber liability insurance policy?
Are you aware of any specific regulatory or industry requirements that apply to your business (for example, PIPEDA or PCI-DSS)?

hero.title: A clear method, not a black box.
hero.body: Security work fails when it stays vague. Here is exactly how we work with you, stage by stage, from the first conversation onward.

items.label: Understand
items.copy: We start by learning how your business actually operates, not by running through a generic checklist. That means your systems, your data, your people, and the way work really gets done every day. A recommendation built on a real picture of your environment is worth far more than one built on assumptions.

items.label: Prioritize
items.copy: Every finding is ranked by real risk and real business impact, not just technical severity. You receive a short, clear list of what matters most first, instead of a lengthy report that never gets opened. For a growing business, this is what turns a security review into something you can actually act on.

items.label: Protect
items.copy: We put the right controls in place for what matters most, whether that means a specific service, a policy change, or ongoing monitoring. Our team works alongside yours so nothing is left as advice sitting on a page. This is where the plan becomes real protection.

items.label: Improve
items.copy: Security is not something you set up once and leave alone. We check in on a regular schedule, report on real progress, and adjust as your business and the threats around it change. What worked last year may not be enough this year, and this stage is how we keep pace.

closing.title: Ready to see exactly where you stand.
